“In this corner: Kris Allen, the guy next door. It is the battle of the acoustic rocker versus the glam rocker. Conway, Arkansas, versus California. The guy next door versus the guy-liner.”

After three performances apiece and plenty of feedback from the judges, Southern California glam rocker Adam Lambert appeared to have the edge—but it did not look that way early in Tuesday’s show.

In the first round, the contestants selected a favorite song from one of their previous performances this season. Simon Cowell declared Kris Allen the winner after Allen performed “Ain’t No Sunshine” on the piano.

Watch Allen and Lambert talk after the show ».

Lambert chose to sing “Mad World,” wearing a long black coat as he walked around a stage filled with white smoke—a presentation Cowell found “over-theatrical.”

“I think ‘Mad World’ is kind of symbolic,” Lambert told reporters after the show. “It talks about people who don’t feel like they fit in.”

The second round featured songs hand-picked by “American Idol” creator Simon Fuller. Lambert shed the black overcoat and belted out Sam Cooke’s “A Change Is Gonna Come” while wearing a shiny silver suit.

Paula Abdul told Lambert, “It was the best I’ve ever heard you sing, ever!”

Allen received far less flattering feedback after performing Marvin Gaye’s classic “What’s Goin’ On” in the second round.

See the best and worst performances from season eight ».

“I thought it was too laid-back for a night like this,” Cowell said before awarding the second round to Lambert.

The third round featured a twist: Both contestants had to sing “No Boundaries,” a song co-written by judge Kara DioGuardi.

Lambert performed first and had little difficulty with the ballad. Afterward, Cowell told the 27-year-old, “You have been one of the best, most original contestants we’ve ever had on the show.”

Allen, however, struggled to stay in tune throughout his performance, though the judges were less critical this time.

“You have thoroughly, thoroughly deserved to be standing on that stage tonight. Congratulations,” Cowell said.

Watch anchors debate “Idol” finalists ».

After the show, Lambert told reporters that the contestants had not had much time to work on “No Boundaries,” making it something of a “rush job.”

“There was a lot of lyric, and it was a big song,” Lambert said. “But it’s a beautiful song.”

It seems almost fitting that the two are facing off in the finale. According to Allen, he and Lambert were once roommates during the competition. They even critique each other’s rehearsals.

“He’s always giving me stuff to change about mine ... to make it better,” Allen told reporters.

# Lambert, Allen offer contrasting visions in ‘American Idol’ finale

**Adam Lambert brought theatrical power, while Kris Allen relied on understated musicianship in the season eight performance finale.**

**LOS ANGELES** — “American Idol” finalists Adam Lambert and Kris Allen made their closing arguments Tuesday night with three songs apiece, highlighting the sharp contrast that defined the season’s final showdown.

Lambert, the flamboyant rock vocalist known for his soaring range and dramatic stage presence, opened with a reprise of Tears for Fears’ “Mad World.” Performing in a long coat amid moody lighting and fog, he delivered the haunting arrangement that had become one of his signature moments of the competition.

Allen countered with “Ain’t No Sunshine,” accompanying himself on piano and giving the Bill Withers classic a restrained, intimate treatment. The performance played to Allen’s strengths: conversational phrasing, careful dynamics and an ability to reshape familiar songs without overpowering them.

For the second round, producer Simon Fuller selected the songs. Lambert tackled Sam Cooke’s civil rights-era anthem “A Change Is Gonna Come,” building from a controlled opening to a forceful finish. Allen performed Marvin Gaye’s “What’s Going On,” using guitar and a relaxed arrangement that emphasized his singer-songwriter identity.

The finalists then faced the same challenge: “No Boundaries,” the season’s coronation song. Lambert delivered the anthem with characteristic intensity, though its phrasing and range made for an uneven fit. Allen’s version was also strained in places, underscoring the difficulty of a song neither contestant had chosen.

The judges largely framed the night as a clash of styles rather than a runaway victory. Lambert offered the bigger spectacle and the most technically ambitious vocals. Allen presented a quieter alternative built on interpretation, warmth and musical subtlety.

That contrast had carried both singers through the season. Lambert emerged as the competition’s theatrical risk-taker, drawing on glam rock and arena-sized vocals. Allen, initially a lower-profile contestant, steadily gained momentum with acoustic arrangements and an accessible, contemporary sound.

When the votes were announced the following night, Allen was named the season eight winner, completing one of the show’s most notable underdog runs. Lambert finished second, but the finale made clear that both contestants had established distinct artistic identities — and that their post-“Idol” careers would not be defined by the result alone.

**Kris Allen and Adam Lambert Make Final Case in ‘American Idol’ Performance Show**

*May 19, 2009 — Los Angeles*

Kris Allen and Adam Lambert closed the eighth season of *American Idol* with a sharply contrasting final performance night, turning the Nokia Theatre stage into a contest between Allen’s understated musicianship and Lambert’s theatrical vocal power.

Each finalist performed three songs Tuesday: a reprise selected from earlier in the season, a song chosen by series creator Simon Fuller and “No Boundaries,” the season’s coronation single, co-written by judge Kara DioGuardi.

Lambert opened by returning to his haunting version of Tears for Fears’ “Mad World.” Dressed in a long coat and surrounded by fog and stark lighting, he again emphasized the performance’s dark, dramatic character. The arrangement had earned unusual praise earlier in the season, but Simon Cowell was less enthusiastic about the finale reprise, calling it “a little bit over-theatrical” and comparing its presentation to *The Phantom of the Opera*.

Allen countered with “Ain’t No Sunshine,” seated at the piano and delivering the Bill Withers song with a restrained arrangement that built in intensity. The performance drew one of Cowell’s strongest endorsements of the night.

“I wasn’t sure America had made the right choice last week,” Cowell told Allen, referring to the vote that put him in the final. “I take all that back after that performance.”

Cowell awarded the first round to Allen, giving the Arkansas singer an early advantage in the judges’ running assessment.

### Lambert answers with Sam Cooke classic

For the second round, Fuller selected Sam Cooke’s civil-rights-era standard “A Change Is Gonna Come” for Lambert. The choice allowed the 27-year-old Los Angeles performer to move from a controlled opening into the kind of soaring upper-register vocals that had defined his season.

Paula Abdul called it Lambert’s best performance, telling him, “That was the best I’ve ever heard you sing,” and describing the moment as “iconic.”

Cowell was similarly emphatic. “You are 100 percent back in the game,” he said, effectively giving Lambert the second round.

Fuller chose Marvin Gaye’s “What’s Going On” for Allen. Performing with his guitar, Allen gave the song an acoustic, relaxed treatment. Abdul praised his artistic identity, but Cowell argued that the arrangement lacked the scale expected from a finale performance. He likened it to “three friends in their bedroom strumming along to Marvin Gaye” and said it was too laid-back for such an important night.

The criticism highlighted the central contrast between the finalists. Lambert treated the finale as a major theatrical event, while Allen remained committed to the intimate, singer-songwriter style that had carried him through the competition.

### Both finalists struggle with “No Boundaries”

The final round placed both singers on equal ground with “No Boundaries,” a new song written by DioGuardi, Cathy Dennis and Mitch Allan. The inspirational anthem proved demanding for both contestants, with its dense lyrics and high vocal range.

Lambert sang first, bringing power and control to the climactic sections, though the song did not showcase his originality as effectively as “A Change Is Gonna Come.” Cowell largely set aside criticism of the composition and instead reviewed Lambert’s season as a whole, calling him “one of the best, most original contestants” the program had ever had.

Abdul also looked beyond the single performance, telling Lambert that his career would continue regardless of the vote. “We’ll be seeing you next week and many years after that,” she said.

Allen then performed the same song in a lower key. He appeared to strain in portions of the melody, and the judges agreed that “Ain’t No Sunshine” had been his strongest moment of the evening. Cowell nevertheless told Allen that he had earned his place in the finale, saying, “You thoroughly deserve to be standing on this stage tonight.”

At the end of the broadcast, neither contestant made a lengthy closing speech, instead urging viewers to vote. Allen, who had entered the finale as the less heralded of the two, emphasized his gratitude for reaching the last show. Lambert likewise thanked the audience and judges, presenting the contest as the culmination of a season rather than a personal rivalry.

### A finale built on contrasting identities

The performance show offered no clear consensus winner. Allen appeared to take the opening round, Lambert dominated the second, and the shared finale song did little to separate them. Cowell suggested that Lambert had won the night overall, but Allen’s first performance remained one of the episode’s most warmly received moments.

The matchup was also notable for its lack of visible antagonism. Allen and Lambert repeatedly praised each other during the season and presented themselves as friends with different musical approaches rather than bitter competitors.

The public vote ultimately favored Allen. On the results broadcast the following night, May 20, host Ryan Seacrest announced him as the season-eight winner. Visibly stunned, Allen responded by praising his fellow finalist: “Adam deserves this.”

Lambert finished as runner-up but received the judges’ clearest prediction of future stardom. The final performance episode therefore ended as the season had unfolded: Allen succeeding through subtle arrangements and emotional directness, and Lambert leaving the stage as one of the show’s most distinctive vocal and theatrical performers.

# Acoustic Rocker Versus Glam Rocker: Kris Allen and Adam Lambert Face Off in the *American Idol* Finale

The eighth-season finale of *American Idol* presented viewers with one of the show’s sharpest stylistic contrasts: understated acoustic rocker Kris Allen against flamboyant glam rocker Adam Lambert.

During the May 19, 2009, performance show at the Nokia Theatre in Los Angeles, each finalist sang three songs—a reprise of a favorite earlier performance, a selection chosen by show creator Simon Fuller, and “No Boundaries,” the season’s coronation single.

## Round One: Contestants’ Choice

Lambert opened by returning to his eerie, theatrical version of Tears for Fears’ “Mad World.” The performance displayed the soaring vocals and dramatic staging that had made him the season’s most conspicuous showman, although Simon Cowell thought the presentation was slightly overdone.

Allen answered with Bill Withers’ “Ain’t No Sunshine,” accompanying himself on piano and delivering the intimate, soulful style that had fueled his late-season rise. The judges praised his confidence and musicianship.

**Round result:** Cowell awarded the first round to Allen.

## Round Two: Simon Fuller’s Choice

For Lambert, Fuller selected Sam Cooke’s civil-rights-era classic “A Change Is Gonna Come.” Lambert began with restraint before building toward a powerful, high-register climax. It was an ideal vehicle for his range and theatrical intensity, and the judges responded enthusiastically.

Allen received Marvin Gaye’s “What’s Going On.” His arrangement was relaxed and acoustic, emphasizing warmth over spectacle. Although the performance fit his identity, the judges felt it was too subdued for a finale and lacked the impact of Lambert’s song.

**Round result:** Lambert clearly took round two, leaving the contest effectively tied after two performances each.

## Round Three: “No Boundaries”

Both finalists then performed “No Boundaries,” written by judge Kara DioGuardi with Cathy Dennis and Mitch Allan. As the designated winner’s single, its lyrics focused on perseverance, ambition and overcoming obstacles.

The song proved difficult for both singers. Lambert attacked it with his customary vocal power, but the melody and inspirational-pop format did not always sit naturally with his glam-rock style. Allen’s arrangement felt closer to contemporary pop-rock, though the key pushed him toward the upper limits of his range.

The judges offered mixed assessments rather than declaring an unambiguous third-round victor. Many observers felt Allen’s tone fit the recording better, while Lambert gave the more technically forceful performance. Cowell concluded by telling Lambert that he had been one of the best and most original contestants the program had ever had, but he stopped short of a simple round-three ruling.

## An Aftershock Before the Show

The finale unfolded against a literal tremor in Los Angeles. Hours before the live broadcast, an earthquake of roughly magnitude 4.0 to 4.1 shook the area. It was identified as an aftershock of the magnitude-4.7 earthquake that had struck near Inglewood two days earlier.

The aftershock was felt around Los Angeles, including near the finale venue, but it caused no significant damage and did not interrupt the broadcast.

## The Final Result

When the public vote was announced the following night, Allen defeated Lambert and became the eighth *American Idol* champion. The result was widely viewed as an upset: Lambert had often appeared to be the season’s front-runner, while Allen had advanced through consistency, musical rearrangements and an increasingly strong connection with voters.

Allen subsequently released “No Boundaries” as his coronation single; Lambert’s version was also made available. The finale remains memorable not only for its close competition, but for the contrast at its center—the quiet acoustic interpreter versus the spectacular glam-rock vocalist.

- **Lambert:** “Mad World,” Sam Cooke’s “A Change Is Gonna Come,” and the coronation single “No Boundaries.”
- **Allen:** “Ain’t No Sunshine,” Marvin Gaye’s “What’s Going On,” and “No Boundaries.”

Rehearsal and dress-rehearsal assessments largely anticipated what happened on the live show: Lambert appeared vocally commanding and theatrical, while Allen offered a quieter, more intimate approach. The chief concern was “No Boundaries,” which sounded awkwardly pitched and difficult for both singers, although Allen’s version was generally considered a somewhat better stylistic fit.

### Judges’ feedback

The judges praised Allen’s opening “Ain’t No Sunshine.” Simon Cowell said Allen had fully justified his place in the finale and awarded him the first round. Allen’s “What’s Going On,” however, divided the panel: Randy Jackson and Simon found it too restrained for a finale, with Simon comparing it to friends casually playing in a bedroom.

Lambert’s “Mad World” drew praise for its vocals but criticism from Simon for being overly theatrical. His performance of **“A Change Is Gonna Come”** became the night’s biggest judges’ favorite. Randy said Lambert could “sing his face off,” Paula Abdul described him as headed toward iconic status, and Simon said he was “100 percent back in the game,” giving Lambert the second round.

Neither finalist received unqualified praise for “No Boundaries.” The judges noted pitch and range problems, but Kara DioGuardi—who co-wrote the song—urged viewers not to judge the contestants solely by that number. Simon closed by calling Lambert one of the most original and memorable contestants the program had produced, while telling Allen that he deserved to be on the stage.

### After the show

Backstage, neither singer indulged in predictions or attacks. Lambert emphasized that he and Allen were friends and very different artists, making direct comparisons difficult. Allen similarly praised Lambert’s talent and said he would be pleased for him if he won. Their post-show comments reinforced the impression created onstage: Lambert was the flamboyant vocal powerhouse, Allen the understated musician, but personally they remained supportive rather than antagonistic.

The vote remained open overnight. Allen was announced as the Season 8 winner the following evening, with Lambert finishing second.
